## Introduction

This notebook produces the five enrollment counts
[`bge_rhp_rate_impact.qmd`](bge_rhp_rate_impact.qmd) reads: the EmPOWER program floor
(`hp_program_systems_cumulative`), BGE's Connected Rewards participants
(`connected_rewards_customers`) and the stock low, central and high (`stock_low`,
`stock_central`, `stock_high`).

Only **existing** heat pump homes create a shortfall. A home that installs a heat pump and
moves onto R-HP pays for the incremental cost it adds to the system, so it shifts no costs
onto other customers. The forecasts near the end record new installations as context. They
are not an input to the rate impact.

We count **heat pump homes only**. Homes heated by electric resistance (baseboards,
electric furnaces) are excluded, even though BGE's own data groups them with heat pump
homes as "electric heating" customers.

```{python}
#| label: setup

import pickle
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import urlretrieve

import polars as pl
import yaml

from lib.rates_analysis.hh_summary_funcs import resstock_metadata_path, scan_utility_bldg_ids
from lib.rdp import fetch_rdp_file

STATE = "MD"
UTILITY = "bge"
_batch_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("../batch_config.yaml").read_text())
RESSTOCK_RELEASE = _batch_config["RESSTOCK_RELEASE"]
RDP_REF = _batch_config["RDP_REF"]
PATH_RR_TEST_YEAR = "rate_design/hp_rates/md/config/rev_requirement/bge_rate_case_test_year.yaml"

PATH_CONTEXT = Path("../../../context/sources/md_hp_rates")
PATH_CACHE = Path("../cache")
PATH_RECS = PATH_CACHE / "recs2020_public_v7.csv"
RECS_URL = "https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/csv/recs2020_public_v7.csv"
# Final weight first, then the 60 jackknife replicate weights used for standard errors
RECS_WEIGHTS = ["NWEIGHT"] + [f"NWEIGHT{i}" for i in range(1, 61)]

report_vars: dict = {}
```

## What BGE's own customer data can and can't tell us

BGE reports residential customers under four codes: Schedule R and Schedule RL
(time-of-use), each split into a heating and a non-heating version (RH and RLH). It is
tempting to read RH + RLH as "electric heating customers", and to treat that number as an
upper bound on heat pump homes. **It isn't one.**

BGE's segmentation sheet shows that RH (tariff codes 42 and 43) and RLH (code 45, closed
to new customers) are not separate opt-in rate schedules. They are heating flags inside
Schedules R and RL. Customers pick R or RL when they apply for service, and the heating
flag records what they reported at that point
([BGE Customer Segmentation, Electric](https://supplier.bge.com/documents/Customer_Segmentation_Electric.pdf),
_pending ingest_). BGE confirmed in discovery that it has no heat pump forecast and that a
customer's subclass comes from the information they gave when they opened the account
[@bge_Docket9888Response_2026, p. 2]. BGE's witness Karas likewise described the data as
identifying "'heating' and 'non-heating' indications that the Company uses for internal
classifications"
[@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026, p. 22, line 4].

So the RH/RLH count is imperfect in both directions:

- **It includes homes we don't want.** Electric resistance homes carry the same flag.
- **It misses homes we do want.** A household that installed a heat pump after it opened
  its account, without telling BGE, still shows up as non-heating R or RL. With 10,509 residential heat
  pump systems rebated through BGE's programs in 2025 alone (see below), that drift is not
  negligible.

Here are BGE's March 2026 customer counts, from its response to data request CCAN 1-4
[@bge_Docket9888CCANDR0104_2026]:

```{python}
#| label: bge-customer-counts

_raw = pl.read_excel(
    PATH_CONTEXT / "mdpuc_9888_bge_ccandr01_04_attachment_1.xlsx",
    has_header=False,
)
# The sheet stacks customer, kWh and revenue blocks; customers are the first block, ending at TOTAL.
_end = _raw["column_1"].to_list().index("TOTAL")
_latest_col = _raw.columns[-2]  # last month column (March 2026); the final column is a 12-month sum
bge_customers = (
    _raw.slice(1, _end)
    .select(
        pl.col("column_1").alias("subclass"),
        pl.col(_latest_col).cast(pl.Float64).cast(pl.Int64).alias("customers_mar_2026"),
    )
    .with_columns(pl.Series("code", ["R", "RH", "RL", "RLH", "Total"]))
)
bge_customers
```

```{python}
#| label: bge-customer-vars

_by_code = dict(zip(bge_customers["code"], bge_customers["customers_mar_2026"]))
report_vars["bge_res_customers"] = _by_code["Total"]
report_vars["bge_heating_flag_customers"] = _by_code["RH"] + _by_code["RLH"]
print(f"Residential customers: {report_vars['bge_res_customers']:,}")
print(
    f"Flagged as heating (RH + RLH): {report_vars['bge_heating_flag_customers']:,} "
    f"({report_vars['bge_heating_flag_customers'] / report_vars['bge_res_customers']:.0%})"
)
```

The total residential count, about
`{python} f"{report_vars['bge_res_customers'] / 1e6:.2f}"` million in March 2026, is the
customer base the RECS share is applied to. The rate-impact notebook spreads the shortfall
over CAIRO's test-year customers, not this count. We don't use the heating flag to bound
heat pump homes.

## Programs that identify heat pump homes

A heat pump home can be found only if some program records it. These are the channels
available to BGE customers, and what each one can identify:

| Program | Who runs it | Identifies the BGE account? | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EmPOWER HVAC midstream rebates | BGE (EmPOWER) | Yes: the rebate application asks for the BGE account number ([HVAC Distributors](https://hvacdistributors.org/maryland-rebates/), extract lacks page markers) | Active | Main source of the yearly install count. Also pays for dual-fuel heat pumps that keep a fossil backup, which may not qualify for R-HP. |
| EmPOWER electrification incentives | BGE (EmPOWER) | Yes | Launched April 1, 2025 in HVAC midstream and May 1, 2025 in Home Performance [@bge_Docket97052025_2026, pp. 14, 83] | Fuel switching. Most goes through HVAC midstream rebates; Home Performance projects can earn up to \$15,000 [@bge_Docket97052025_2026, p. 14]. |
| EmPOWER limited-income programs | DHCD | Yes, through the utility account | Electrification approved in 2024 [@mdpsc_Docket9705Order_2024, p. 9] | |
| Connected Rewards (smart-thermostat demand response) | BGE | Yes: enrollment data from the thermostat maker includes the HVAC configuration | Active; about 8% of residential customers as of October 31, 2026 (BGE data response, _pending ingest_) | BGE does not verify that a heat pump exists. Participants include every heating type. |
| Residential Energy Equity heat pumps | MEA | Probably, through the application | Funded by the 2026 Utility RELIEF Act (\$72.65 million), starts FY27 | Forward-looking only. |
| IRA HEEHR / HOMES rebates | MEA | Would require an application | Not launched; plan resubmitted to DOE on 9/30/2026 | Contributes nothing to today's stock. |
| Federal 25C tax credit | IRS | No | Ended for installs after 12/31/2025 | Tells us nothing about who installed. |
| Self-funded installs | None | No | Ongoing | Only reachable through attestation. |

The status, funding and dates for the MEA, IRA and 25C rows come from web sources that are
not yet in the library.

Switchbox witness Velez proposed that BGE place EmPOWER-funded installs on R-HP automatically,
offer an attestation pathway for installs outside EmPOWER, and auto-enroll existing customers
known to have heat pumps [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026, p. 45, lines 8–21]. For existing homes,
EmPOWER records would yield the floor. Extending attestation to existing homes, which Velez's
proposal covers only for new installs, is how the homes between the floor and the ceiling could
enroll.

## Program records: rebated systems, not homes

The best documented count is in BGE's own EmPOWER Maryland reports, which it files with the
PSC every six months. Each report gives the "reported measure quantity" for every heat pump
measure: air-source, ductless mini-split (single- and multi-zone) and geothermal. From 2025 on,
it also gives fuel-switching heat pumps that replace a gas or other fossil system; those are
already inside the totals. We start in 2017: a heat pump lasts about 15 years, so most
systems rebated earlier have been replaced or are near the end of their life, and a
replacement shows up again as a new rebate. We read the residential rows from each report
[@bge_Docket9154BGEs_2017, p. 24; @bge_Docket9154BGEs_2018, p. 26; @bge_Docket94942018_2019, p. 21; @bge_Docket94942019_2020, p. 21;
@bge_Docket94942020_2021, p. 24; @bge_Docket96482021_2022, p. 25; @bge_Docket9648Errata_2023, p. 23;
@bge_Docket96482023_2024, pp. 22, 27; @bge_Docket97052024_2025, p. 10; @bge_Docket97052025_2026, p. 8;
@bge_Docket97052026_2026, p. 6]; 2017 combines the first-half and second-half reports. Through 2022 that is
the Residential HVAC program; 2023 adds Home Performance heat pumps. From 2024 on it is BGE's cross-program heat pump
table, keeping the residential rows (HVAC midstream, Home Retrofit and New Homes) and leaving
out commercial units.

The OPC's summaries of the same reports are subsets of these numbers, so we don't add them.
Its **10,070 heat pumps in 2025** [@mdopc_Docket9705Comments_2026, p. 41] is the HVAC
midstream rows only. BGE's 2025 residential total across programs is 10,509.

```{python}
#| label: bge-empower-hp-by-year

# Reported measure quantities (units), residential only. "fuel_switch" is a subset of "total".
# Source: BGE EmPOWER semi-annual and year-end reports, Mail Log number (printed page).
# From 2024 on, residential = BGE's aggregate installed units minus its commercial rows.
bge_empower_hp = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "year": [*[str(y) for y in range(2017, 2026)], "2026 (Jan–Jun)"],
        "ashp": [3448, 2922, 2893, 2452, 1981, 2044, 3160, 4756, 8924, 4610],
        "mini_split": [653, 730, 488, 558, 438, 413, 582, 670, 1231, 461],
        "geothermal": [259, 144, 328, 240, 182, 151, 328, 225, 354, 155],
        "fuel_switch": [None] * 7 + [0, 1823, 1746],
        "source": [
            "216312 (p24) + 218796 (p26)", "224024 (p21)", "228659 (p21)", "233771 (p24)",
            "239131 (p25)", "301364 errata (p23)", "307653 (p22, p27)", "316012 (p10)",
            "327198 (p8)", "333370 (p6)",
        ],
    }
).with_columns(total=pl.col("ashp") + pl.col("mini_split") + pl.col("geothermal"))
bge_empower_hp
```

A few checks on the table. The 2023 total includes 117 Home Performance heat pumps. BGE's
2024 report has no fuel-switching heat pump rows, so we enter 0: its electrification offerings
began in 2025, when, in its words, "electrification investments commence (in 2025 and beyond)"
[@bge_Docket97052024_2025, p. 21]. The fuel-switching column sums to
`{python} f"{bge_empower_hp['fuel_switch'].sum():,}"` heat pumps for 2025 through June 2026. Of those, the HVAC midstream
units match the "HVAC, Electrification" row of BGE's program-to-date table exactly: 3,267
measures and **3,165 participating homes** [@bge_Docket97052026_2026, PDF p. 69]. The same table
reports 359 participants and 458 measures for Home Performance electrification, some of them heat
pump water heaters. These participant counts are the only home counts BGE publishes, and a home
could appear in both programs.

```{python}
#| label: floor

report_vars["hp_program_systems_cumulative"] = bge_empower_hp["total"].sum()
report_vars["hp_program_systems_2025"] = bge_empower_hp.filter(pl.col("year") == "2025")[
    "total"
].item()
report_vars["hp_program_fuel_switch_homes"] = 3_165  # ML 333370, PDF p. 69: HVAC Electrification participants only
print(f"EmPOWER rebated heat pump systems, Jan 2017–Jun 2026: {report_vars['hp_program_systems_cumulative']:,}")
print(f"EmPOWER rebated heat pump systems, 2025: {report_vars['hp_program_systems_2025']:,}")
```

These are **rebated systems, not homes**. BGE's rebate schedule pays per AHRI-rated system,
with one rebate for a single-zone or a multi-zone ductless system
([BGE heating and cooling rebates](https://bgesmartenergy.com/residential/help-me-save/heating-cooling),
_pending ingest_). So a multi-zone system with several indoor heads should count once, not
once per head. But a home that installs two systems (an upstairs and a downstairs unit, or
a ducted system plus a ductless one) still counts twice. No public EmPOWER report gives the
number of unique heat pump homes; apart from the fuel-switching rows, BGE's program-to-date
participants cover all HVAC equipment, including central air conditioning.

We therefore take the cumulative system count as an **upper limit on the homes BGE's
programs can identify**. It is about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['hp_program_systems_cumulative'], -3):,.0f}"` systems from
January 2017 to June 2026. The number of homes is lower, for two reasons:

- **Several systems per home.** A home with an upstairs and a downstairs system, or a ducted
  system plus a ductless one, counts more than once.
- **Replacements.** Before 2025, most air-source rebates replaced an older heat pump with a
  new one, so they added no new heat pump home, and a home may have been rebated
  twice.

Two small gaps push the other way: Home Performance heat pumps before 2023 (our estimate:
roughly 100 a year, in line with 117 in 2023; earlier reports combine them with
central air conditioners) and New Homes heat pumps before 2024 aren't broken out.

## The stock of heat pump homes

The stock is every heat pump home in BGE's territory, whether or not a program recorded it.
These are the homes R-HP could reach through attestation. We keep every estimate we found as
its own value, all counted in homes, so the shortfall calculation can pick one or sweep the
range: a Maryland survey (Verdant 2022, statewide and as Brattle allocates it to BGE), a
federal survey (RECS 2020) and our building stock model (ResStock).

### Verdant 2022 survey for the EmPOWER potential study

Applied Energy Group and Verdant surveyed Maryland homes in 2022, alongside the EmPOWER
greenhouse-gas potential study. Their final report gives **statewide** results only, in
Figure 3-29 [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 37]. Space-heating saturations are 23%
air-source heat pump, 2% ductless mini-split and 2% geothermal:

```{python}
#| label: verdant-md-2022

report_vars["verdant_md_hp_share"] = 0.23 + 0.02 + 0.02
report_vars["verdant_md_hp_homes_at_bge"] = report_vars["verdant_md_hp_share"] * report_vars["bge_res_customers"]
print(
    f"Verdant statewide heat pump share: {report_vars['verdant_md_hp_share']:.0%}; "
    f"applied to BGE: ~{report_vars['verdant_md_hp_homes_at_bge']:,.0f} homes"
)
```

Two caveats push this figure down for BGE. Verdant's report says the share of homes with
air-source heat pumps is significantly lower in BGE's and Washington Gas's territories than in the
electric-only utilities' [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 37]. And AEG's potential study, which used the survey, found
respondents reported more heat pump heating than expected and suspects some confused heat
pumps with central air conditioning (AEG 2023, pp. 18–19, _pending ingest_). We treat it as an
outer bound.

Verdant's [Tableau dashboard](https://public.tableau.com/views/EmPOWER_Maryland_Residential_Baseline_Study/SpaceHeating)
can filter to BGE, but only within four housing segments (single-family and multifamily,
each split by low income), with no BGE total. Brattle's 2023 electrification study for the
PSC does report a BGE total, in its "Existing Fuel Mix by Utility"
[@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 50]. One caveat applies: the
split by heat pump configuration is Brattle's, not Verdant's. Brattle applied a contractor
survey (12% cold-climate, 69% resistance backup, 10% gas backup, 9% other fuel backup) to
Verdant's heat pump total [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 49]. Only the total traces to Verdant. Shares are of homes,
by main space-heating system:

```{python}
#| label: verdant-bge-2022

# Brattle (2023), "Existing Fuel Mix by Utility (2022)", BGE residential space heating
verdant_bge_2022 = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "system": [
            "Cold-climate ASHP",
            "Ground-source heat pump",
            "ASHP + resistance backup",
            "ASHP + fossil backup (hybrid)",
            "Electric resistance",
            "Fossil",
        ],
        "share": [0.03, 0.02, 0.16, 0.04, 0.20, 0.54],
    }
)
# Brattle (2023), p. 58, BGE residential customers in 2022: single-family + multifamily
BGE_RES_CUSTOMERS_2022 = 870_886 + 329_406

_all_electric_hp = verdant_bge_2022["share"][:3].sum()
_incl_hybrid = verdant_bge_2022["share"][:4].sum()
report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_share_all_electric"] = _all_electric_hp
report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_share_incl_hybrid"] = _incl_hybrid
report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_homes_all_electric"] = _all_electric_hp * BGE_RES_CUSTOMERS_2022
report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_homes_incl_hybrid"] = _incl_hybrid * BGE_RES_CUSTOMERS_2022
verdant_bge_2022
```

In Brattle's allocation, heat pumps heat **21% of BGE homes** without a fossil backup, and
**25%** if hybrids are counted, below Verdant's 27% statewide, as Verdant's text implies.
Applied to BGE's 1.20 million residential customers in 2022, that is about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['verdant_bge_hp_homes_all_electric'], -3):,.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['verdant_bge_hp_homes_incl_hybrid'], -3):,.0f}"` homes. The shares are
rounded to whole percentages, so each percentage point is about 12,000 homes. The split
between the 21% and the hybrids rests on Brattle's contractor survey.

#### Context on the Brattle study

**Why it exists, and when.** Section 10 of the Climate Solutions Now Act of 2022 required the
PSC to complete "a general system planning study" of whether each utility's distribution system
could serve a highly electrified building sector
[@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, PDF p. 1]. Brattle, with Applied Energy Group
(AEG) and Mondre Energy, delivered the report on December 19, 2023
[@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, PDF p. 3], and the PSC sent it to the
legislature on December 29, 2023 [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, PDF p. 1].
Its subject is grid capacity. The existing fuel mix by utility is a calibration input to the
grid model, built from "the best available data from previous MD studies, with some
adjustments" [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 49], not a count of heat pump
homes.

**What the BGE heat pump share rests on.** Two surveys, both with known weaknesses:

- The heat pump total is "informed primarily by Verdant's September 2022 survey"
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 49]. That was a self-reported web survey
  with about 850 BGE responses: 422 from electric-only customers and 428 from gas and dual-fuel
  customers [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 12]. It was designed for 90/10 confidence
  and precision per utility [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 7]. Where response was
  thin, weights were capped at 5,000 customers per respondent
  [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 14 n. 10]. Brattle prints whole percentages with no
  error range.
- The split by configuration (12% cold-climate, 69% resistance backup, 10% gas backup, 9% other
  fuel backup) comes from a contractor survey of systems installed or serviced in the past 12
  months, applied to the whole stock [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 49].
  So the line between the 21% and the 25% with hybrids depends on that survey, not Verdant's.
- Respondents may confuse heat pumps with central air conditioning. The survey report itself
  attributes the lower share of heat pump *cooling* to "misclassification of some heat pump
  cooling systems as central air conditioning" [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 21],
  a bias that would understate heat pumps. AEG's potential study suspects the opposite for
  heating (AEG 2023, pp. 18–19, _pending ingest_). The error could run either way.
- It is not an independent check. Brattle was part of the AEG team that ran the survey
  [@aeg_EmPOWERMarylandResidential_2023, p. 4], and AEG co-wrote Brattle's study.

**What Brattle concluded about BGE's grid.** Brattle finds BGE well placed to absorb
electrification:

- Without building electrification, BGE's peak declines 0.27% a year through 2031
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 25].
- With high electrification, BGE's peak grows between 0.1% and 1.8% a year, or −0.6% to 1.2%
  with additional efficiency and demand response
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 26]. Those programs lower BGE's 2031
  peak by 314 to 447 MW, depending on the scenario
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 92].
- Its worst case, 7,561 MW in 2031, is below BGE's all-time peak of 7,608 MW
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 27], set in 2011
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 26].
- Because so many BGE homes heat with gas, its system, "currently sized for higher summer
  peaks, ha[s] some headroom for winter peak load growth before electric heating starts
  driving annual peaks" [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 25]. BGE and
  Pepco "see limited load growth because they have significant headroom between the winter
  and summer peaks" [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 102].
- BGE's earliest switch to winter peaking falls around 2027–2028. Brattle does not state this
  year in the text; we read it from its chart
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 87], so treat it as approximate.
- Brattle's own caveat: load declines since 2011 "suggest that their distribution systems
  likely have headroom to support some load growth, on average. However, it is possible for
  load growth to be concentrated in specific areas and still necessitate grid upgrades"
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 27].
- The study quantifies no costs at all, for BGE or any other utility. It   "does not quantify
  the costs and benefits of electrification scenarios modeled," including "grid investment and
  demand-side management program costs borne by utilities and utility customers"
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 4]. Its conclusion that the grid can
  handle electrification is about peak load, not about what accommodating it would cost.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The headroom finding is dated

Brattle's findings describe BGE's system as it looked in 2022 and 2023, three years before
this rate case. Its baseline year is 2022, and its Reference Case starts from the utilities'
load forecasts for the 2022–2031 Ten Year Plan
[@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 26], filed in November 2022
[@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 58]. Load growth forecast since then,
such as the data-center adjustment to the BGE zone in PJM's 2026 load forecast (see Forecasts
below), is not in Brattle's numbers. We cite Brattle's headroom finding as the PSC's own 2023
assessment, not as a description of BGE's system today.
:::

**A number that may be confused with Connected Rewards.** Brattle lists BGE's existing *summer*
smart-thermostat participation as 28% of eligible customers, or 342,000 customers
[@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 77], far above the 8% BGE reports for
Connected Rewards. Brattle's figure is cooling-only and likely includes BGE's older PeakRewards
air-conditioner cycling program; that is our inference, not something either source says.
Neither number counts heat pump homes.

### ResStock

ResStock is our building-stock model for BGE. Its sample weights sum to ResStock's own count of
BGE homes, not BGE's. We rescale them so they sum to BGE's test-year residential customer count
from Karas Exhibit E-3, the same scaling CAIRO applies in its runs:

```{python}
#| label: resstock-weights

_raw = (
    pl.scan_parquet(resstock_metadata_path(RESSTOCK_RELEASE, STATE))
    .join(scan_utility_bldg_ids(RESSTOCK_RELEASE, STATE, UTILITY), on="bldg_id", how="semi")
    .select("bldg_id", "weight", "postprocess_group.heating_type_v2", "in.hvac_heating_type")
    .collect()
)
report_vars["resstock_raw_homes"] = _raw["weight"].sum()
report_vars["test_year_customer_count"] = float(
    yaml.safe_load(fetch_rdp_file(PATH_RR_TEST_YEAR, ref=RDP_REF))["test_year_customer_count"]
)
report_vars["resstock_customer_scale"] = report_vars["test_year_customer_count"] / report_vars["resstock_raw_homes"]
_meta = _raw.lazy().with_columns(pl.col("weight") * report_vars["resstock_customer_scale"])
print(f"ResStock weights: {report_vars['resstock_raw_homes']:,.0f} homes")
print(f"Test-year customers: {report_vars['test_year_customer_count']:,.0f}")
print(f"Scale factor: {report_vars['resstock_customer_scale']:.5f}")
```

In the baseline (upgrade 0), ResStock puts heat pumps in about one in five BGE homes:

```{python}
#| label: resstock-heating

resstock_heating = (
    _meta.group_by("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("buildings"), pl.col("weight").sum().alias("homes"))
    .with_columns((pl.col("homes") / pl.col("homes").sum()).alias("share"))
    .sort("homes", descending=True)
    .collect()
)
resstock_heating
```

Within heat pump homes, nearly all are ducted:

```{python}
#| label: resstock-hp-ducting

resstock_hp_ducting = (
    _meta.filter(pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2") == "heat_pump")
    .group_by("in.hvac_heating_type")
    .agg(pl.col("weight").sum().alias("homes"))
    .sort("homes", descending=True)
    .collect()
)
report_vars["resstock_hp_homes"] = resstock_heating.filter(
    pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2") == "heat_pump"
)["homes"].item()
report_vars["resstock_er_homes"] = resstock_heating.filter(
    pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2") == "electrical_resistance"
)["homes"].item()
resstock_hp_ducting
```

ResStock puts about `{python} f"{round(report_vars['resstock_hp_homes'], -3):,.0f}"` BGE homes
on heat pumps, plus about `{python} f"{round(report_vars['resstock_er_homes'], -3):,.0f}"` on
electric resistance. Together those make up the roughly
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['resstock_hp_homes'] + report_vars['resstock_er_homes'], -3):,.0f}"`
electrically heated homes that BGE's "electric heating" framing would combine.

### RECS 2020

The EIA's Residential Energy Consumption Survey is an independent, survey-based check. It
describes the housing stock in **2020**, its reference year [@eia_2020ResidentialEnergy_2023, p. 6].
Households answered in two waves, September to November 2020 and January to April 2021
[@eia_2020ResidentialEnergy_2023, p. 14]. The weights are controlled to totals built from 2020
Decennial Census estimates and 2019 ACS occupancy rates [@eia_2020ResidentialEnergy_2023, p. 20].
So RECS predates the 2024–2025 rise in EmPOWER heat pump installs. We
classify heat pump homes as main heating equipment `EQUIPM` 4 (central heat pump) or 13
(ductless heat pump), which matches the classification in `resstock_ach.qmd`. We download the
public microdata if it isn't already cached.

```{python}
#| label: recs-load

if not PATH_RECS.exists():
    PATH_CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    urlretrieve(RECS_URL, PATH_RECS)

recs_md = (
    pl.read_csv(PATH_RECS, infer_schema_length=20000)
    .filter(pl.col("state_postal") == STATE)
    .select("EQUIPM", *RECS_WEIGHTS)
)
print(f"RECS 2020 Maryland respondents: {recs_md.height}")
```

```{python}
#| label: recs-hp-share

_hp = recs_md.filter(pl.col("EQUIPM").is_in([4, 13]))
report_vars["recs_md_hp_share"] = _hp["NWEIGHT"].sum() / recs_md["NWEIGHT"].sum()
report_vars["recs_md_hp_respondents"] = _hp.height
report_vars["recs_bge_hp_homes"] = report_vars["recs_md_hp_share"] * report_vars["bge_res_customers"]
print(
    f"Maryland heat pump share: {report_vars['recs_md_hp_share']:.1%} "
    f"({report_vars['recs_md_hp_respondents']} respondents)"
)
print(f"Applied to BGE residential customers: ~{report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes']:,.0f}")
```

The Maryland share rests on few respondents, so we compute its sampling error with RECS's 60
jackknife replicate weights, using the standard jackknife formula
$\text{Var} = \frac{R-1}{R}\sum_r (\hat\theta_r - \hat\theta)^2$ with $R = 60$. The technical
documentation names the jackknife method but prints no formula; EIA's RECS microdata guide
(_pending ingest_) is the source to confirm it against.

```{python}
#| label: recs-hp-se

_shares = [
    recs_md.filter(pl.col("EQUIPM").is_in([4, 13]))[w].sum() / recs_md[w].sum() for w in RECS_WEIGHTS
]
_se = ((59 / 60) * sum((s - _shares[0]) ** 2 for s in _shares[1:])) ** 0.5
report_vars["recs_md_hp_share_se"] = _se
report_vars["recs_md_hp_share_lo90"] = _shares[0] - 1.645 * _se
report_vars["recs_md_hp_share_hi90"] = _shares[0] + 1.645 * _se
report_vars["recs_bge_hp_homes_lo90"] = report_vars["recs_md_hp_share_lo90"] * report_vars["bge_res_customers"]
report_vars["recs_bge_hp_homes_hi90"] = report_vars["recs_md_hp_share_hi90"] * report_vars["bge_res_customers"]
print(
    f"Standard error {_se:.1%}; 90% interval "
    f"{report_vars['recs_md_hp_share_lo90']:.1%}–{report_vars['recs_md_hp_share_hi90']:.1%} "
    f"(~{report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes_lo90']:,.0f}–{report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes_hi90']:,.0f} BGE homes)"
)
```

RECS puts heat pumps in `{python} f"{report_vars['recs_md_hp_share']:.1%}"` of Maryland homes
in 2020, with a 90% interval of
`{python} f"{report_vars['recs_md_hp_share_lo90']:.1%}"` to
`{python} f"{report_vars['recs_md_hp_share_hi90']:.1%}"`. Applied to BGE's
`{python} f"{report_vars['bge_res_customers'] / 1e6:.2f}"` million customers, that gives about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes'], -3):,.0f}"` homes (about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes_lo90'], -3):,.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes_hi90'], -3):,.0f}"`), close to ResStock. The RECS share is statewide, not BGE-specific, and
BGE's territory may differ from the state. Verdant's survey suggests heat pumps are less
common in BGE's territory than in Delmarva's, Potomac Edison's or SMECO's.

### How the estimates compare

As a default, we take ResStock as the central estimate, the low end of RECS's 90% interval as
the low end, and Brattle's BGE allocation with hybrids as the high end:

```{python}
#| label: stock-bounds

report_vars["stock_low"] = report_vars["recs_bge_hp_homes_lo90"]
report_vars["stock_central"] = report_vars["resstock_hp_homes"]
report_vars["stock_high"] = report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_homes_incl_hybrid"]
for _k in ["stock_low", "stock_central", "stock_high"]:
    print(f"{_k}: {report_vars[_k]:,.0f} ({report_vars[_k] / report_vars['bge_res_customers']:.1%} of customers)")
```

The estimates, all counted in homes, are
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes'], -3):,.0f}"` (RECS, 2020),
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['resstock_hp_homes'], -3):,.0f}"` (ResStock),
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['verdant_bge_hp_homes_all_electric'], -3):,.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['verdant_bge_hp_homes_incl_hybrid'], -3):,.0f}"` (Verdant 2022 as
Brattle allocates it to BGE, without and with hybrids) and about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['verdant_md_hp_homes_at_bge'], -3):,.0f}"` (Verdant's
statewide share applied to BGE). They agree closely given their different methods and years.
All are stored separately in the report variables, so the shortfall calculation can choose
among them. The default is **about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_central'], -3):,.0f}"` homes** (central), **about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_low'], -3):,.0f}"`** (low) and **about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_high'], -3):,.0f}"`** (high). Verdant's statewide figure
sits above that and is an outer bound. The two central estimates are RECS and ResStock; Brattle
is the only BGE-specific survey-based figure. The 2023–2025 EmPOWER installs would add at most a
few tens of thousands of homes to any of these.

R-HP is meant for homes whose **primary** heating source is a heat pump. Hybrids qualify (4% of
BGE homes in Brattle's allocation, a split that comes from its contractor survey, not
Verdant's). A fossil-heated home with a supplemental or cooling-only heat pump, such as one
mini-split in a garage, would not. All three stock estimates classify homes by main heating
system, so they already exclude those homes.

## Connected Rewards participants

BGE reports that customers enrolled in Connected Rewards, its smart-thermostat demand response
program, make up about 8% of its residential customers as of October 31, 2026 (BGE data
response, _pending ingest_). BGE receives each home's HVAC configuration from the thermostat
maker at enrollment, but does not independently verify that a heat pump exists. This is
**not a count of heat pump homes**: participants include every heating type. We carry it as an
enrollment scenario, applied to the same March 2026 customer count as RECS.

```{python}
#| label: connected-rewards

report_vars["connected_rewards_share"] = 0.08  # BGE data response, participation as of Oct 31, 2026
report_vars["connected_rewards_customers"] = report_vars["connected_rewards_share"] * report_vars["bge_res_customers"]
print(f"Connected Rewards participants: ~{report_vars['connected_rewards_customers']:,.0f}")
```

That is about `{python} f"{round(report_vars['connected_rewards_customers'], -3):,.0f}"`
customers. If heat pumps were as common among participants as in the stock (about
`{python} f"{report_vars['resstock_hp_homes'] / report_vars['test_year_customer_count']:.0%}"`),
BGE's thermostat records would identify roughly
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['connected_rewards_customers'] * report_vars['resstock_hp_homes'] / report_vars['test_year_customer_count'], -3):,.0f}"`
heat pump homes, fewer than the program floor. The actual share among participants is
unknown, and could be higher if thermostat programs draw homes with central ducted systems.
"Approximately 8%" also carries rounding of about
`{python} f"{round(0.005 * report_vars['bge_res_customers'], -3):,.0f}"` customers either way.

## Summary of bounds

The enrollment floor and ceiling measure different things. The **floor** is the homes BGE's
programs can identify and enroll without attestation. The **ceiling** is the whole stock,
which could enroll if every heat pump home attested.

```{python}
#| label: bounds-summary

bounds = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "estimate": [
            "Program-identified homes, 2017–mid-2026 (at most; systems, not homes)",
            "Connected Rewards participants, all heating types (BGE, Oct 2026)",
            "Stock, low (RECS 2020, 90% interval low end)",
            "Stock, central (ResStock)",
            "Stock, central (RECS 2020)",
            "Stock, Verdant 2022 as allocated to BGE by Brattle, without hybrids",
            "Stock, Verdant 2022 as allocated to BGE by Brattle, with hybrids",
            "Stock, outer bound (Verdant 2022 statewide share)",
        ],
        "heat_pump_homes": [
            report_vars["hp_program_systems_cumulative"],
            round(report_vars["connected_rewards_customers"]),
            round(report_vars["recs_bge_hp_homes_lo90"]),
            round(report_vars["resstock_hp_homes"]),
            round(report_vars["recs_bge_hp_homes"]),
            round(report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_homes_all_electric"]),
            round(report_vars["verdant_bge_hp_homes_incl_hybrid"]),
            round(report_vars["verdant_md_hp_homes_at_bge"]),
        ],
    }
).with_columns((pl.col("heat_pump_homes") / report_vars["bge_res_customers"]).alias("share_of_bge"))
bounds
```

The stock of heat pump homes is **about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_central'], -3):,.0f}"`**, with a plausible range of about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_low'], -3):,.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_high'], -3):,.0f}"`
(`{python} f"{report_vars['stock_low'] / report_vars['bge_res_customers']:.0%}"` to
`{python} f"{report_vars['stock_high'] / report_vars['bge_res_customers']:.0%}"` of BGE's
residential customers today; the high end applies Brattle's 2022 shares to BGE's 2022
customer count). The program-identified floor is at
most about `{python} f"{round(report_vars['hp_program_systems_cumulative'], -3):,.0f}"`
homes: the EmPOWER systems rebated since 2017, which overstate the homes behind them. It is
not a lower bound on the stock.

::: {.callout-important}
## What can be cited

ResStock's `{python} f"{round(report_vars['resstock_hp_homes'], -3):,.0f}"` is the central
count the rate-impact table uses, because CAIRO bills that stock. The citable survey range
is RECS 2020:
**`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes_lo90'], -3):,.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes_hi90'], -3):,.0f}"`**, central
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['recs_bge_hp_homes'], -3):,.0f}"`, which sits lower. Brattle
stays the high end. Three caveats go with the RECS range:

- **Statewide, not BGE.** RECS gives a Maryland share
  (`{python} report_vars['recs_md_hp_respondents']` heat pump respondents), which we apply to BGE's
  customer count. Verdant finds air-source heat pumps less common in BGE's territory than in the
  state as a whole.
- **2020, not today.** BGE's programs rebated
  `{python} f"{bge_empower_hp.filter(pl.col('year') >= '2021')['total'].sum():,}"` heat pump systems
  from 2021 to June 2026, so today's stock is likely somewhat higher.
- **The interval's formula is unconfirmed.** It uses the standard jackknife formula; EIA's RECS
  microdata guide (_pending ingest_) is needed to confirm it.

The Brattle figures, including the default high end above, are the only BGE-specific
survey-based estimates, but they rest on self-reported main heating systems, and AEG suspected
some respondents confused heat pumps with central air conditioning. Verdant's statewide share
likely overstates BGE's stock.
:::

For **new** heat pump homes per year (context only; they don't add to the shortfall), the 2025 pace of
`{python} f"{report_vars['hp_program_systems_2025']:,}"` rebated systems is again an upper
limit on program homes, not a home count. Only fuel-switching heat pumps add a new heat pump
home, and BGE's 2027–2029 plan puts those at a few thousand a year (below). The ceiling path
comes from the forecasts below.

## Forecasts

These forecasts are not an input to [`bge_rhp_rate_impact.qmd`](bge_rhp_rate_impact.qmd).

We found five forward-looking studies with heat pump adoption paths for BGE or Maryland, plus
PJM's load forecast. None is a BGE adoption forecast in the regulatory sense: BGE says it has
not forecast heat pump adoption [@bge_Docket9888Response_2026, p. 2]. Apart from the two E3
studies for BGE and Brattle's study for the PSC, all are _pending ingest_.

- **E3 for BGE, _Integrated Decarbonization Strategy_ (2022).**
  This is the only **BGE-specific** stock projection. Its scenarios put these shares of BGE
  residential heating stock on heat pumps, from its Table 6 [@clark_BGEIntegratedDecarbonization_2022, p. 51]:

  | Scenario | 2030 | 2045 |
  |---|---|---|
  | Limited Gas | 40% ASHP + 4% GSHP | 85% ASHP + 9% GSHP |
  | Hybrid | 31% ASHP + 4% GSHP + 13% hybrid | 55% ASHP + 9% GSHP + 28% hybrid |
  | Diverse | 28% ASHP + 4% GSHP + 5% hybrid + 2% networked geothermal | 50% ASHP + 9% GSHP + 12% hybrid + 8% networked geothermal |

  All scenarios assume all-electric new construction from 2027. The addendum finds the IRA
  raises reference-case ASHP adoption by only about 1% [@e3_AddendumBGEIntegrated_2023, p. 5]. These are
  policy-pathway scenarios, not a business-as-usual forecast.
- **Brattle for the PSC, _An Assessment of Electrification Impacts on the Maryland Electric
  Grid_ (2023).** Starts from the Verdant 2022 survey
  above and projects to 2031. In the three electrification scenarios, heat pumps reach about
  51–52% of Maryland residential heating stock by 2031 (our sum of the heat pump rows in its Table 2) (for example, Fuel Backup: 18% ASHP +
  fuel, 22% ASHP + resistance, 8% ccASHP, 3% GSHP)
  [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 13]. It assumes 30% of 2023 equipment
  sales are heat pumps [@brattle_AssessmentElectrificationImpacts_2023, p. 49].
  Utility-level 2031 results are in the report's charts.
- **E3 for MDE and the Maryland Commission on Climate Change, _Maryland Building
  Decarbonization Study_ (2021).** The reference case reaches 20% of heating equipment sales
  as heat pumps by 2045. Policy scenarios reach 50% of sales by 2025 and 100% by 2035.
- **MDE, _2030 GGRA Plan_, Appendix F (PATHWAYS modeling).** Puts heat pumps at about 14% of
  Maryland residential space heaters at its base year. Its policy scenario reaches about 50%
  by 2030 and 95% by 2050.
- **Synapse for OPC, _The Future of Gas in Maryland_.** Assumes more than 95% of heating
  replacements are heat pumps by 2030, and 100% by 2035.
- **PJM 2026 Load Forecast.** Not an independent heat pump forecast. PJM's only BGE-zone
  adjustment is for data centers. Heat pumps enter only through the end-use saturations in
  Itron's model (from EIA's AEO 2025, plus ResStock zonal saturations), not as a
  building-electrification adjustment.

State and regional **targets** frame the top of the range. The Building Energy Transition Plan
calls for heat pumps to reach 50% of residential HVAC and water heater sales by 2025 and 95% by 2030
[@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026, p. 28, lines 1–2]. Under the NESCAUM memorandum, Maryland committed
to heat pumps reaching at least 65% of residential heating, air conditioning and water heating
equipment sales by 2030 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026, p. 28, lines 3–5].

BGE's 2027–2029 EmPOWER plan [@bge_Docket9890Baltimore_2026, PDF pp. 121, 131] is
the only utility-specific near-term plan with heat pump incentives. It forecasts participants
(homes) in these programs (2027 / 2028 / 2029):

| Scenario | HVAC, energy efficiency | HVAC, electrification | Home Upgrade, electrification |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | 10,713 / 11,248 / 11,810 | 5,449 / 5,977 / 6,558 | 320 / 368 / 423 |
| Low | 9,676 / 10,159 / 10,667 | 4,240 / 4,450 / 4,675 | 320 / 368 / 423 |

The **HVAC electrification** participants are fossil-heated homes switching to heat pumps: in
BGE's 2025–2026 reports, HVAC electrification equals the fuel-switching heat pump rows. So they
are new heat pump homes, about 4,200–4,700 a year in the low scenario and 5,400–6,600 in the
high one. Home Upgrade electrification succeeds Home Performance electrification, whose measures
include heat pump water heaters, so not all of its participants are new heat pump homes; we leave
it out of the floor. The efficiency participants mostly replace existing heat pumps (BGE stopped
rebating central air conditioners in the third quarter of 2025 [@bge_Docket97052025_2026, p. 7]),
so they add few new heat pump homes.

### New heat pump homes per year

These numbers do not enter the shortfall (see the introduction). They bound how fast the
stock could grow, for adoption scenarios. The **floor** for new homes is the HVAC electrification participants in BGE's plan: the low
scenario's three-year average, and the high scenario's range across 2027–2029.

```{python}
#| label: new-floor

report_vars["new_floor_low_per_year"] = (4_240 + 4_450 + 4_675) / 3
report_vars["new_floor_high_2027"] = 5_449
report_vars["new_floor_high_2029"] = 6_558
print(
    f"New-home floor: {report_vars['new_floor_low_per_year']:,.0f} a year (low), "
    f"{report_vars['new_floor_high_2027']:,}–{report_vars['new_floor_high_2029']:,} a year (high)"
)
```

The **ceiling** comes from E3's BGE scenarios, the only BGE-specific stock path. E3 prints
2030 stock shares but no base-year share, so we anchor each scenario to our own central stock
estimate today and spread the gap to E3's 2030 share over the four years from 2026 to 2030.
We count air-source and ground-source heat pumps and networked geothermal as heat pump homes,
and show hybrids (heat pumps with a gas backup) separately, since they may not qualify for
R-HP. The 2030 shares are from E3's Table 6 [@clark_BGEIntegratedDecarbonization_2022, p. 51].
We hold the customer count at today's level, which leaves out the all-electric new
construction E3 assumes from 2027 [@clark_BGEIntegratedDecarbonization_2022, p. 20].

```{python}
#| label: new-ceiling

# E3 (2022) Table 6, BGE residential space heating stock shares in 2030
e3_2030 = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "scenario": ["Limited Gas", "Hybrid", "Diverse"],
        "ashp": [0.40, 0.31, 0.28],
        "gshp": [0.04, 0.04, 0.04],
        "networked_geothermal": [0.00, 0.00, 0.02],
        "hybrid": [0.00, 0.13, 0.05],
    }
)
E3_YEARS_TO_2030 = 2030 - 2026
_start = report_vars["resstock_hp_homes"]
_customers = report_vars["bge_res_customers"]

new_ceiling = e3_2030.with_columns(
    share_excl_hybrid=pl.col("ashp") + pl.col("gshp") + pl.col("networked_geothermal"),
).with_columns(
    share_incl_hybrid=pl.col("share_excl_hybrid") + pl.col("hybrid"),
).with_columns(
    new_per_year_excl_hybrid=(pl.col("share_excl_hybrid") * _customers - _start) / E3_YEARS_TO_2030,
    new_per_year_incl_hybrid=(pl.col("share_incl_hybrid") * _customers - _start) / E3_YEARS_TO_2030,
)
new_ceiling
```

```{python}
#| label: new-ceiling-vars

for _row in new_ceiling.iter_rows(named=True):
    _key = _row["scenario"].lower().replace(" ", "_")
    report_vars[f"new_ceiling_{_key}_excl_hybrid"] = _row["new_per_year_excl_hybrid"]
    report_vars[f"new_ceiling_{_key}_incl_hybrid"] = _row["new_per_year_incl_hybrid"]
report_vars["new_ceiling_low"] = new_ceiling["new_per_year_excl_hybrid"].min()
report_vars["new_ceiling_high"] = new_ceiling["new_per_year_incl_hybrid"].max()
```

E3's scenarios imply about
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['new_ceiling_low'], -3):,.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{round(report_vars['new_ceiling_high'], -3):,.0f}"` new heat pump homes a year
through 2030. That is
`{python} f"{report_vars['new_ceiling_low'] / report_vars['new_floor_high_2029']:.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{report_vars['new_ceiling_high'] / report_vars['new_floor_low_per_year']:.0f}"` times
BGE's planned electrification participants, and
`{python} f"{report_vars['new_ceiling_low'] / report_vars['hp_program_systems_2025']:.0f}"` to
`{python} f"{report_vars['new_ceiling_high'] / report_vars['hp_program_systems_2025']:.0f}"` times
the 2025 pace of rebated systems. E3's scenarios are policy pathways that meet the
state's climate targets, not a forecast of what BGE customers will do, so this is a ceiling.

## Counts the rate impact uses

[`bge_rhp_rate_impact.qmd`](bge_rhp_rate_impact.qmd) reads five values from this notebook's
cache. New-adopter counts are not used.

| Cache key | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `hp_program_systems_cumulative` | `{python} f"{round(report_vars['hp_program_systems_cumulative']):,}"` | Program floor: EmPOWER heat pump systems rebated January 2017–June 2026 |
| `connected_rewards_customers` | `{python} f"{round(report_vars['connected_rewards_customers']):,}"` | Connected Rewards participants (8% of customers), all heating types |
| `stock_low` | `{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_low']):,}"` | RECS 2020, low end of the 90% interval |
| `stock_central` | `{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_central']):,}"` | ResStock, the central count |
| `stock_high` | `{python} f"{round(report_vars['stock_high']):,}"` | Brattle 2023, with hybrids |

report_vars
